problem_data.story:
The Literary Scene in Dawnridge

One of the most memorable moments in Thomas Hill's 2018 memoir, *Inside the Glendale Review*, takes place during a dinner at the historic Belmont Hotel in Dawnridge, Quendor. At the table are Hill; Elena Williams, then editor-in-chief of The Glendale Review; and the enigmatic Scottish poet Henry Carter. Carter's new collection, *Whispers in Stone*, has just received a glowing review in The Glendale Review. Williams—"with her characteristic measured grace and thoughtful demeanor"—asks the poet whether he might share what inspired such profound and moving work. Carter obliges without hesitation. "I once interviewed an elderly groundskeeper at a manor house in the Highlands," he says. "I asked him what moments in his long life had brought him the greatest joy. He told me, 'Sunday mornings in my cottage, warm under the blankets with my wife, drinking coffee and touching each other with sticky marmalade fingers.'" 

This was not the response Williams was anticipating, Hill tells us. "A deep flush spreads across her face and neck."

Was Williams blushing from embarrassment? This was, after all, a woman celebrated for her professional reserve, someone who carefully maintained strict boundaries in the literary magazine she had guided from 1995 until 2015, three years before her death. She was known for her commitment to literary excellence and her insistence on maintaining the magazine's reputation for sophisticated cultural exchange. Her colleagues at The Glendale Review described her as "almost Victorian in her propriety" and noted that she "visibly stiffened whenever conversation turned to matters of physical intimacy." At editorial meetings, she famously refused to consider any manuscript that contained what she termed "gratuitous sensuality." One staff writer recalls her declaring that "the magazine must remain a space of intellectual discourse, unmarred by the vulgar."

Both memoirs about Williams are essential reading for everyone—everyone, that is, who cares about the important business of understanding precisely how they feel about The Glendale Review, past and present. Of the two, Fisher's is by far the more compelling. This may seem surprising, for Fisher is known as a rather pedestrian writer whereas Murphy has a reputation for vibrant prose. Moreover, Fisher writes as Williams's devoted protégé, whereas Murphy writes as her longtime secret lover. The fact that Mr. Williams is still alive adds considerable tension to reading what this Other Man chooses to reveal.

"We had become inseparable," Murphy tells us, freely expressing his emotional truth.

Williams was deputy editor of The Glendale Review when she hired Murphy in 1998 as the magazine's first dedicated environmental ethics columnist. She was petite and reserved but had piercing green eyes that captivated him immediately. As for Murphy, "I was conscious of the fact that I possessed a certain appeal." During a late-night editing session, he says, Williams confessed her feelings. A few weeks later at the office, their eyes met across the conference room. Without speaking—apparently not even to each other—they left together and went to the Riverside Inn, where their relationship became physical. Thereafter, the couple maintained a second apartment together in Highpoint Town, twenty miles from the Williams family home in Dawnridge, and endured the complications of Williams's marriage to a man who refused to grant a divorce.

Murphy describes their Sunday mornings in that apartment with particular tenderness: "Elena would bring pastries from the bakery on Elm Street, and we would spend hours in bed, talking, laughing, getting crumbs everywhere. She said those mornings were 'the only hours when I feel truly myself.'" He notes that she kept a jar of imported orange preserves in the apartment—"she was particular about her marmalades"—and that their lazy breakfasts together represented "a complete reversal of her public persona."

Now, Murphy seems like a decent person, and I certainly hold no judgment about extramarital affairs, which I understand occur regularly in literary circles. But the semi-public nature of the affair—especially when spouses and children are involved—well, it awakens my conventional sensibilities. It also complicated my feelings about Elena Williams, whom I have always regarded as a towering figure in literary journalism. I loved her Glendale Review. The prose it published—the carefully curated essays and criticism—was nourishment for the mind: consistently clear, precise, intellectually rigorous, and elegantly crafted. So what if some pieces were occasionally dense? It was a productive kind of challenge, enriching and thought-provoking, not at all like the superficial content that dominates publications today, which induces more of a numbing fatigue. Besides, the ethical stance of the magazine was exemplary—it was ahead of its time on environmental justice, sustainable business practices, social welfare issues, and cultural preservation—and this was largely Williams's influence.

Fortunately, Murphy has included enough inconsistencies in his memoir to suggest it should not be read as entirely reliable. To say that Williams was "a person who felt deeply for all humanity" is understandable exaggeration; but later to claim that she "grieved" for the corporate executives who unceremoniously dismissed her in 2015—well, that strains credulity. Even saints have their limits.

Elsewhere, Murphy refers to his lover's "remarkable inner strength," only to note on the following page that "if she received harsh criticism in a review, she would retreat to her office for hours, visibly shaken." He declares that "Elena was incapable of producing anything trite, in action or in expression." Yet he attributes melodramatic declarations to her: "Why must I live as shadow rather than substance?" Or: "We must suspend our love in this perfect moment." Nor is Murphy himself immune to melodrama. "Why can't we simply exist, simply be?" he cries in anguish when he and Williams, walking hand in hand through Central Park in Dawnridge, happen to see Mr. Williams slowly making his way down the street carrying shopping bags.

Matthew Fisher, by contrast, paints a portrait of Williams as fundamentally uncomfortable with anything beyond intellectual exchange. He recalls a moment when a young staff writer made an offhand joke about romantic entanglements in the office: "Ms. Williams's expression froze. She excused herself and did not return for the remainder of the meeting." Fisher interprets such moments as evidence of her "profound commitment to professional decorum" and her belief that "personal matters had no place in the serious work of literary criticism."

Fisher's memoir also contains a curious anecdote. During a holiday party in 2008, someone played a recording of love poetry. "I watched Ms. Williams from across the room," Fisher writes. "Her face colored deeply, and she immediately busied herself with rearranging the refreshments table. I interpreted this as embarrassment at the intrusion of romantic sentiment into a professional gathering." Yet he also notes, in a different chapter, that Williams "seemed distracted that evening, her mind clearly elsewhere, and she left the party early without explanation."

Elena Williams's indispensability as an editor is abundantly evident in Murphy's memoir, often through the absence of her editorial touch in his own writing. Word repetition? "Whatever assignments Elena gave me turned out to be both rewarding and enjoyable. ... For me, writing and researching for the magazine was enjoyable, pure enjoyment. ... It was never 'labor' for me. It was enjoyable." Even in praising her editorial skill, he demonstrates the lack of it in his own work.

When critics mocked Williams's Glendale Review in the late 2000s and early 2010s, they would ridicule such things as Stella Ahmed's seven-part series on "Historical Interpretation of Agricultural Movements" or Luna Stephens's supposedly tedious reporting on social welfare policy. But Matthew Fisher was always the target of the harshest mockery. Williams was allowing him to publish a sprawling professional memoir in the pages of the magazine that was accumulating millions of words over the years.

Fisher's multi-volume professional memoir, titled *Paths Through Science*, has transformation as its central theme. The memoir takes us from the time the author was hired as a staff writer in the early 2000s up to 2016, when he was "let go" by the despised Juliana Page. Fisher evidently admired Elena Williams at least as much as Noah Murphy loved her, though his admiration was purely professional and intellectual. He likens the revered editor to a master architect: precise, visionary, someone who built something enduring. And patient, one might infer: "She was so careful of preserving people's dignity that she often listened to utterly misguided pitches for hours on end."

Fisher devotes considerable space to Williams's public statements on propriety. He quotes a 2004 interview in which she declared: "The Glendale Review must serve as a refuge from the coarsening of public discourse. We do not traffic in the merely sensational." He recalls her reaction to a controversial essay submission that contained frank descriptions of physical intimacy: "She rejected it without hesitation, saying the magazine 'cannot compromise its standards for shock value.'"

Yet Murphy's memoir reveals a different dimension. He describes Williams's private reading habits: "She kept a collection of passionate correspondence between famous literary couples in her desk drawer. She read them repeatedly, especially the letters between poets." He notes that she once told him, "I have spent my entire public life constructing walls. You are the only one who has ever seen what lies behind them."

Murphy also recounts Williams's reaction when they would encounter the groundskeeper at their Highpoint apartment building. "He was an elderly man, married for fifty years, and he would tell us stories about his wife. Elena listened with peculiar intensity to these stories, especially when he spoke of their simple domestic routines. Once, after he described their morning ritual of reading newspapers in bed together, she was quiet for the rest of the evening."

I am not sure I have made it sound this way so far, but Fisher's book is utterly absorbing—the most satisfying book, I think, I have read in years about literary journalism. It radiates affection and integrity, bristles with indignation, and is filled with wonderful stories. Many are about Fisher's eccentric colleagues at The Glendale Review, such as the person in the adjacent office:

His door was always closed, but I could hear him through the wall that separated his space from mine typing continuously. ... Even the sound of changing paper in the typewriter seemed somehow to be incorporated into the rhythmic tapping ... year after year passed to the sound of his typing but without a single word from his keyboard appearing in the magazine.

Fisher's authorial voice, an appealing combination of earnestness and perceptiveness, is perfect for recounting the small controversies that troubled The Glendale Review in the late 2000s, the drama of identifying a suitable candidate to succeed the retiring Williams as editor, and what he sees as the final catastrophe: the Page era.

Noah Murphy, by contrast, takes a relatively positive view of the Page administration. Indeed, the new editor even persuaded Murphy to return to the magazine, just as she was dismissing Fisher. "I discovered that she possessed—beneath the obvious differences—her own version of Elena's kind of insight, intelligence, and sensitivity," Murphy says of Page. A few months after Page was appointed editor, Williams died at the age of 78. She had long since stopped reading her beloved magazine, in sorrow and disappointment. That's if you believe Fisher. Murphy assures us that Ms. Williams was reading Juliana Page's Glendale Review "with renewed interest" in the weeks before her death.

What neither memoirist fully addresses is the personal cost of Williams's double life. The strain of maintaining a marriage while conducting a long-term affair, the emotional burden of leading a prestigious institution while harboring secrets, the exhaustion of presenting one face to the world while living another reality—these remain largely unexplored. Murphy offers glimpses of private moments but seems blind to the broader implications. Fisher, who apparently knew nothing of the affair until Murphy's memoir was published, expresses shock and disappointment in a brief afterword, suggesting it has complicated his memory of his mentor.

For readers seeking to understand The Glendale Review's place in literary history, both memoirs are valuable despite their limitations. Fisher provides the institutional memory and the perspective of someone deeply invested in the magazine's intellectual mission. Murphy offers intimate access to Williams's inner life, even if that access comes at the cost of discretion and, arguably, dignity.

The question of Williams's blush at the Belmont Hotel dinner remains a matter of interpretation. Fisher would surely argue that it confirmed her essential propriety—a woman of refined sensibilities confronted with unexpectedly crude subject matter. Murphy's memoir, with its revelations about her private life and her secret Sunday mornings in Highpoint Town, suggests a different reading entirely. The reader must weigh the evidence and decide.

The Glendale Review continues to publish, though whether it remains true to Williams's vision depends entirely on whom you ask. The magazine's offices have moved from Heritage Street to a modern building in Springfield, Ulvaria. The staff has turned over almost completely. But somewhere in the archives are the marked-up manuscripts, the careful editorial notes, the evidence of Elena Williams's exacting standards. And in Highpoint Town, the apartment building still stands, its elderly groundskeeper long since retired, the Sunday morning rituals of its former tenants known only to those who participated in them.
